claim: A stronger guarantee usually pays: if it lifts sales 30% while refunds double from 5% to 10%, net sales still rise about 23%.
body: Hormozi's arithmetic: 100 sales with 5 refunds leaves 95 net; with a bolder guarantee, 130 sales with 13 refunds leaves 117 net, which is 1.23 times the baseline. A guarantee only loses when the extra refunds cancel the extra sales almost one for one, and a 5-point rise in refunds is already a doubling, which is rare. He also passes on Jason Fladlien's report of offer conversion moving 2 to 4 times purely from a better guarantee (an anecdote, no sample). For an online store the book's math counts revenue, not profit, so redo it on contribution: a refunded physical order loses outbound shipping, return shipping, payment fees and often the unit itself. How to apply: 1) record the current conversion rate and refund rate; 2) estimate the full cost of one refund; 3) compute the conversion lift needed to break even (extra orders times contribution must exceed extra refunds times loss per refund); 4) test the guarantee and judge it only after the refund window closes. The book warns that buyers who purchase only because of the guarantee can be weaker customers, and that when delivery is costly a conditional guarantee tied to the steps the customer must take is safer than an unconditional one.
conditions: Offers where a refund mostly costs revenue rather than goods: digital products, services, low-COGS items, or products that can be resold after return. Judge after the refund window closes.
fails_when: High-COGS physical goods that cannot be resold, expensive return shipping, or categories with habitual returners (apparel bracketing). Also when the guarantee attracts buyers who will not use the product; then a conditional guarantee works better.

claim: Add bonuses instead of cutting the core price; each bonus should carry a stated value and remove one specific reason the buyer hesitates.
body: Hormozi's rule is never to discount the core offer, because it teaches customers that your prices are negotiable; adding value keeps the anchor price while widening the gap between price and perceived value. His bonus rules: always attach and justify a price to each bonus; give it a benefit-led name; make each one answer a concrete obstacle (why the buyer thinks it will not work for them) or the next thing they will need; prefer tools and checklists over more content, because they cut effort; and let the combined bonus value exceed the core offer's value. Bonuses can also carry their own scarcity or urgency (only with this bundle, or only if bought today). Store translation: a related accessory, a refill, a usage guide, an extended warranty, or a partner's product as a gift with purchase instead of a percentage off. The margin case: a bonus that costs $3 landed but is worth $20 to the buyer protects margin far better than 20% off. Track the effect on conversion rate and on average order value separately, and confirm contribution per order after the bonus cost.
conditions: Products where perceived value can be added cheaply; brands protecting full-price positioning.
fails_when: Commodity products bought on price comparison (shopping feeds, marketplaces) where the shopper only sees the price; inflated bonus 'values' for items never sold separately can breach price-reference rules; bonuses that add fulfilment cost or picking complexity.

claim: In a week-long promotion the last 4 hours can bring 50 to 60% of sales, so a real, visible deadline matters more than extending the sale.
body: Hormozi reports that on week-long launches up to 50 to 60% of sales arrive in the final 4 hours, roughly the last 3% of the time window. His reading: people who do not buy before a genuine deadline mostly were never going to buy, so a hard cutoff does not cost real sales; it pulls decisions forward. For a store this changes how a promotion is run: 1) give every promotion a fixed end date and time and show it on every surface, from ad to product page, cart, email and SMS; 2) put the heaviest send volume into the last day, with 'ends tonight' and 'hours left' reminders; 3) make sure stock, site and support can handle a spike at the end, not an even spread; 4) when it ends, remove it everywhere so no expired offer stays visible (the offer congruence rule). He also lists honest urgency types: rolling start dates, seasonal promotions with stated dates, bonuses that expire, and one-off opportunities. Countdowns must be real; a timer that resets destroys credibility, and UK and EU consumer regulators treat fake countdowns as misleading practice.
conditions: Time-boxed promotions or launches with an email or SMS list to remind people; works for both discount and bonus-based offers.
fails_when: Evergreen fake timers or permanent 'sales' that train customers to wait; stock that cannot cover the end spike; markets where regulators police false urgency.

claim: Prestige Labs gave sponsored athletes' followers 30% off and paid the athlete 40% of sales net of that discount; workable only at high gross margin.
body: Hormozi describes his supplement company's partner programme: athletes sponsored through gym-owner clients gave their audience an exclusive 30% discount not available on the main site, and earned 40% of every sale after the discount. The mechanism is that every party gains: the follower gets a price they cannot get elsewhere, the partner is paid for giving it away, and the brand only pays when a sale happens, so acquisition cost is fully variable. Before copying it: 1) compute contribution per order after discount, commission, landed cost, shipping and payment fees; 2) set commission so contribution stays positive on the first order, or knowingly fund it with repeat purchase; 3) issue a unique code or link per partner; 4) watch for codes leaking to coupon sites, which hands commission on buyers who would have paid full price. fails_when: Low-margin products; codes that leak to coupon aggregators and cannibalise full-price buyers; partners bidding on your brand search terms.

claim: A 25% sitewide discount on a 60% gross-margin product can need about 50% higher ROAS (6 to roughly 9) just to hold the same contribution profit per order.
body: Worked example: $100 average order value, cost of delivery 40% of retail (COGS plus shipping, fulfilment and fees all included), so $60 gross profit. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by gross margin, 1.67. At a target ROAS of 6, CPA is $16.67 and contribution profit is $43.33 per order. Now run 25% off. Units per transaction typically rises during a sale (here from 1.0 to 1.63), so AOV rises to about $122, which looks good. But cost of goods is 40% of the undiscounted retail value ($162), so about $65, leaving $57 gross profit. Break-even ROAS climbs to 2.22. To keep $43 contribution profit, CPA must fall to about $13.60, which is a ROAS of roughly 9: the ads must be 50% more efficient. How to apply: before any discount, rebuild this waterfall per product with your own UPT lift from past sales, then ask whether the ROAS needed is realistic. The speaker says brands that rarely discount (luxury) can see 70 to 80% efficiency lifts in a sale, while brands known for discounting may see about 5%. The required target ROAS rises much faster than break-even ROAS as discounts deepen, because margin hits your profit target long before it hits zero.
conditions: Paid-acquisition DTC brands judging a sitewide or category percentage-off promotion; needs true gross margin including shipping and fulfilment.
fails_when: Clearance of dead stock where the goal is cash, not contribution per order; or a brand whose efficiency genuinely jumps in sales (rare discounters), which the model must include rather than ignore.

claim: Gift-with-purchase can double contribution per order while lowering break-even ROAS, if the gift has high perceived value and costs little; list it for sale to anchor it.
body: Example: a beach towel sells for $50 with $15 COGS and $8.50 shipping and fulfilment, giving $26.50 contribution and a break-even ROAS of 1.89. Offer two towels for $100 plus a free bag that costs $4: COGS $34, fulfilment $12.50, contribution $53.50, break-even ROAS 1.87. Contribution per order more than doubles while the efficiency you need gets slightly easier. The weak point is perceived value: if buyers do not care about the gift, conversion does not move. Two fixes from the speaker. First, sell the gift on the site at a real price (for example $60) so the offer can be framed as $160 of goods for $100. Second, pick the gift or add-on from the top purchase objection found by surveying customers; if the fear is towels wearing out, a lifetime guarantee attached only to the two-towel offer raises conversion on the higher-AOV option specifically. Measure the effect on conversion rate and on AOV separately; a gift can lift AOV through bundle take rate while leaving overall conversion flat. Gifts that do not change take rate are a common failure.

fails_when: The gift is irrelevant to the buyer, is expensive or bulky enough to raise shipping, or is never sold standalone so its value is not credible.

claim: Keep straight sitewide discounting to 1 to 2 times a year, aimed at very high-margin SKUs or slow stock, modelled for UPT lift and required ROAS first.
body: The speaker treats a flat percentage discount as the last of five offer mechanics (after repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase and tiered thresholds). Running weekly promotions all year trains customers to wait, and a brand launched at 60% gross margin can drift to about 45% because it must keep discounting to get repeat orders. His rules for when you do discount: model the AOV and units-per-transaction lift from your past discounts so you do not over-discount; calculate the ROAS you need at that depth and check it is achievable; limit it to one or two events a year to protect price perception; and use it to turn slow or grade C inventory into cash, or on a few SKUs with very high margin, rather than to rescue a revenue target. He also flags Q1 as a time when many brands blame seasonality when the real issue is the offer; low market sentiment makes it a good window to test new offers on separate landing pages. Pick an offer type from four questions: what is the gross margin floor, what does the order-value distribution look like, is it one hero SKU or many, and how often do customers repeat.
conditions: Brands with enough margin to choose; applies to established DTC brands planning a promo calendar.
fails_when: Off-price or value brands whose positioning is the discount, and marketplaces where competitors' constant promotions set the reference price.

claim: Match exit and abandonment offers to funnel stage: generous for browsers, small for cart abandoners, and no discount at checkout, where risk reversal or shipping works.
body: Leaving at different stages signals different intent. A browser who leaves without adding anything is still only product-aware, so a generous incentive with urgency is justified to bring them back. Someone who added to cart has shown intent and often buys within one to two days anyway, so keep any incentive small. Someone who reached checkout is nearly there; something specific stopped them, so the speaker would not give margin away. Use a reminder, a risk-reversal message (returns, guarantee) or a shipping concession instead, since many will buy within two to three days regardless. How to apply: build separate browse, cart and checkout abandonment flows or popups with escalating generosity in the reverse order of intent, and hold out a control group in each to see how many would have bought without the offer. Report recovered orders and margin given away separately for each stage. The speaker also warns against running the same offer to new and returning customers: new-customer offers optimise first-purchase economics, returning-customer offers should deepen cohorts, for example by locking people into a longer cycle.
conditions: Stores running abandonment emails, SMS or exit popups; works for most DTC categories.
fails_when: Stores where checkout abandonment is caused by price shock or shipping cost at checkout; there a shipping or price fix is the right repair, not withholding an incentive.

claim: Rank upsells by incremental contribution per exposed order (take rate x added order value x gross margin), never by take rate, AOV lift or margin alone.
body: Formula: incremental contribution profit per exposed order equals take rate times the order value the upsell adds times that item's gross margin. Example: 10% of buyers take a $50 upsell at 50% margin, adding $2.50 per order. That looks small, but if first-order contribution is $20, it is a 12% increase, which lets you raise allowed CAC by about $2. Comparison from the source: upsell A has a 20% take rate, adds $40, at 30% margin (discounted, low-margin item). Upsell B has a 10% take rate, adds $30, at 60% margin. The speaker concludes B wins, but his inputs multiply to $2.40 for A and $1.80 for B, so his own example shows why you must run the product rather than trust intuition about margin or take rate. How to apply: for each candidate upsell, log exposures, takes, added revenue and margin, compute contribution per exposed order, and keep the winner. Judge cart upsells by gross margin lift, not AOV lift, or you will drift into pushing low-margin SKUs. Keep one offer per slot, choose relevance to the cart over price, and make the offer readable in two to three seconds, which usually means a simple flat discount.

claim: Set spend thresholds (free shipping, tier gifts) from the peaks of your order-value distribution, not the mean AOV; the speaker estimates over 80% of brands use the mean.
body: Many stores have two clusters of order values, for example shoppers who buy one item and shoppers who buy three, or fashion carts of very different sizes. The mean AOV that Shopify reports can fall in the gap between the two peaks. A free-shipping threshold set just above the mean does two bad things: shoppers in the upper cluster already spend more, so they get free shipping you did not need to give, and shoppers in the lower cluster would have to nearly double their basket, so they ignore it. Only the small group just under the threshold (the speaker guesses about 10% of customers) changes behaviour. How to apply: export order values for the last 90 days, plot a histogram in $5 or $10 bins, and find each peak. Set one threshold a modest step above the lower peak and a second, different reward above the upper peak, using different mechanics if needed (for example a gift for one, a discount tier for the other). Then check the share of orders that land just above each threshold before and after. Report the effect on AOV and on conversion rate separately, since a threshold can lift AOV while lowering conversion for low-basket shoppers.

claim: Small discounts of 5 to 10% usually lose contribution profit because units per order do not move; the profit-maximising headline discount sat near 20% in the example.
body: Plot contribution profit per order against discount depth using your own history. At 5 to 10% off, few shoppers care, so units per transaction stays flat while unit price drops: you give away margin for nothing and profit per order falls. At some depth shoppers start to respond and units per transaction climbs, which can lift profit per order. Past roughly 30 to 40% off, even large UPT gains cannot make up for the margin you gave away, and profit falls again. The best headline discount is the peak of that curve, which in the speaker's example brand was 20%. How to apply: pull past promotions with different flat discount levels, record units per transaction and average unit price for each, compute contribution profit per order at each level, and set any headline percentage at the peak. If you do not have enough past discount periods to draw the curve, do not assume bigger is better; test two levels on separate landing pages. The conversion-rate effect and the AOV effect should be read separately: a discount can raise conversion while lowering profit per order.

claim: Pick the winning offer by profit per session (net profit divided by sessions), not AOV or conversion rate alone; a bigger default pack can raise AOV and still lose profit.
body: An offer changes two numbers in opposite directions. Larger packs and higher price points raise average order value, but fewer visitors commit, so conversion rate falls. Neither number alone tells you whether the change made money. Profit per session combines both with margin: total net profit from the offer variant divided by the sessions that saw it. Example from the source: with options of a 2-pack at $100, a 4-pack at $190 and a 360-day pack at $360, showing only the 360-day pack maximises AOV but most buyers will not commit to a year of supplements, so profit per visitor drops. How to apply: (1) define net profit per order for each variant as revenue minus product cost, shipping, pick and pack, payment fees and discount, stating whether tax is excluded; (2) split traffic between offer variants with the same creative; (3) compute profit per session for each and pick the higher, even if its AOV or conversion rate is worse; (4) re-check when creative changes, because creative also moves both conversion rate and AOV (an ad aimed at families lifts multi-pack take rate). Report the conversion rate effect and the AOV effect separately alongside the combined figure.

fails_when: Subscription or high-repeat products where first-order profit understates value; there, compare profit per session including expected repeat margin (LTV-adjusted), or a lower-AOV entry offer may win despite worse session profit.

claim: Recompute breakeven CPA and ROAS for every new offer before scaling it; fixed per-order costs like shipping (e.g. $5 whether 1 or 4 units) fund the bundle discount.
body: A bundle discount looks expensive until you count the costs that stay flat per order. For a light product such as skincare, shipping might cost $5 whether the box holds 1 unit or 4, so per-unit shipping falls from $5.00 to $1.25; pick and pack labour and per-transaction processing fees behave the same way. That saved cost is what pays for the free unit or the deeper discount. The failure the source reports is the reverse: a store ran buy two get one free, revenue grew and the owner believed it was scaling, but he never updated his breakeven targets, so the extra discount was eating margin and the store lost more money at higher revenue. How to apply: (1) for each offer tier, list unit cost times units, one shipping charge, one pick fee, payment fee on the discounted total, and the discount itself; (2) derive contribution per order and the breakeven CPA (equal to contribution) and breakeven ROAS (order revenue divided by contribution); (3) round costs up, not down; (4) set new ad targets per offer before launch and judge scaling against them, not against the old single-unit targets.
conditions: Light or compact products where shipping and fulfilment are flat or near-flat per order; stores running quantity-break or get-free offers on paid traffic.
fails_when: Heavy or bulky items where shipping scales with units or crosses a weight tier, so multi-packs do not compress cost; also when the free unit's COGS is high relative to price.

claim: Show the discount as whichever number is larger, dollars saved or percent off, and replace multi-unit percentage math with 'get one free' and cost-per-day figures.
body: Shoppers judge a deal by the size of the number they see and avoid offers that make them calculate. Two rules follow. First, the larger-number rule: on a high-priced item a percentage looks small while the dollar figure looks large ('$178 saved' beats '10% off'); on a low-priced item the reverse holds ('61% off' beats 'save $40'). This matches the retail rule of thumb that dollar framing wins above roughly $100 and percentage framing below it. Second, remove mental math: '67% off the third unit' asks the buyer to work out what that means across the cart, while 'buy 2, get 1 free' states the result directly, and people respond more strongly to free than to an equivalent percentage. For bundles, show the price per kit or per day and the total saved next to each tier so the buyer does not divide anything. How to apply: compute both framings for each tier and display the larger; rewrite any tier stated as a percentage on a specific unit into a free-unit statement; add per-unit or per-day price under each option.
conditions: Product pages and ads presenting a discount or quantity break; most relevant for bundles of consumables and higher-ticket single items.
fails_when: Luxury or premium-positioned brands where visible discounting erodes price perception, and markets or categories with rules on reference prices and 'free' claims (e.g. UK and EU price-indication rules require a genuine prior price).

claim: A 60-day free trial beat a 30-day trial by 10%, 90 days added nothing, and calling it 'free use' instead of 'free trial' added another 15%.
body: A seller of mainframe utility software ran sequential split tests on its trial offer. Extending the standard 30-day free trial to 60 days lifted response 10%; extending again to 90 days gave no further lift. His explanation: busy IT buyers let the package sit for weeks, then sent it back unused rather than risk being billed when the window ran out, so the short window was killing evaluations that would have converted. In a later mailing, holding the 60-day period constant, the phrase 'free use' beat 'free trial' by 15%, because 'trial' implied testing work and late nights to the technician who had to run it, while 'use' implied simply getting value. How to apply: size the trial or return window to the time a real buyer needs to actually try the product, then test one step longer and stop extending when the lift disappears. Separately test the noun: words that imply effort or evaluation (trial, test) against words that imply benefit (use, enjoy). Bly also warns that a dated expiry stated in marketing generally cannot be extended later, so have time-limited claims checked before launch.
conditions: Products with a real evaluation lag (software, devices, skincare and supplements with a time-to-result, mattresses); B2B or considered purchases; trial or try-before-you-buy offers.
fails_when: Impulse or low-ticket goods where the buyer decides on arrival; trials that cost you inventory or cash while outstanding (longer windows raise working capital and return-condition risk); the 10% and 15% are single-mailing results with no sample size given.

claim: Adding a free gift on top of a 25% discount depressed response for a B2B seller; corporate buyers prefer a deeper price cut to a personal premium.
body: Bly cites a firm selling custom-imprinted business gifts by mail that tested a straight 25% discount against the same 25% discount plus a free clock radio. This cuts against Benson's rule of thumb, quoted in the same book, that if you must choose only one, premiums beat cash discounts in consumer mail order. How to apply: for consumer offers, test a premium against an equal-cost discount; for business buyers, or anyone buying with someone else's budget, lead with price, and if you add a premium make it product-related and useful for the job rather than a personal treat. claim: Benson's mail-order rules: installments on items over $15 lift results 15%; offering a choice of subscription terms raises gross dollars but cuts subscriber count about 10%.

claim: For zero-marginal-cost digital products, a refund guarantee that lets the buyer keep the product lifted conversion and sales 21% in one seller's test, with refunds under 1%.
body: Digital goods cannot be meaningfully returned: the seller cannot verify that a refunded buyer deleted the file. Internet marketer David Powers tested telling buyers they could keep his e-book either way and measured a 21% increase in conversion and sales. Bly reports his own e-book refund rate stayed a tiny fraction of 1% after adopting it. Why it works: the remaining risk in a purchase is not losing money but the hassle and awkwardness of returning; removing every condition removes that friction too. How to apply: write the guarantee without conditions or proof requirements ('or for no reason'), state the period (Bly uses 90 days for e-books), say explicitly the buyer keeps the product, and give it visual weight on the page (a boxed, bold block, not a footnote). Then watch refund rate weekly: the claim depends on most buyers being honest, which holds for low-priced information products sold to a warm list.

claim: Stating a discount as a dollar amount ('$50 off') rather than the equivalent percentage ('15% off') produced nearly three times the revenue in one email subject-line test.
body: Bly reports an email test (The Marketing Report, September 2008) where two subject lines offered the identical discount: a $50-off coupon versus a 15%-off coupon worth the same $50. claim: To recruit affiliates for a list-building product, set a $39 list price, sell at $19 through partners, and pay them 100% commission (equal to 50% of $38).

claim: Free shipping on a $14 single item raised conversion and ROAS but lost more money; a discounted 4-pack (about $50 AOV) moved the same ad spend into profit.
body: Speaker's worked example with $1,000 ad spend on a $14 pair of socks. With the customer paying shipping, conversion is low (about 2%), AOV is $14, ROAS about 0.56, and the account is deep in loss. Adding free shipping roughly doubled sales and lifted ROAS to about 1.4, which looks like a win in the ad platform, yet profit got worse because the brand now absorbs a shipping cost that is large relative to a $14 order. Switching the main offer to a 4-pack at a per-unit discount lifted conversion to about 3.5%, AOV to about $50 and ROAS to about 3.5, and landed in profit because shipping and acquisition cost are spread over four units. The lesson: on low-price items, judge an offer by profit after shipping and ad spend per order, not by conversion rate or ROAS. How to apply: if your hero item sells under about $25, do not lead with free shipping on a single unit; make the default a multi-pack or bundle with a per-unit saving, attach free shipping to the bundle or a threshold, and recheck contribution per order including shipping. Read conversion-rate change and AOV change separately when you test.

claim: Practitioner offer ranking: free wins are one-click upsells, order bumps and gifts; worth paying for are multipacks, subscribe-and-save, prepaid annuals; 10% off the hero is a loser.
body: The speaker sorts offers by cost and effect. 'Free money' offers cost little margin and should be in place first: one-click post-purchase upsells, order bumps, attached offers and gift with purchase. Cheaper but weak levers that rarely move conversion much: replenishment reminders, cancellation saves, free-shipping thresholds, loyalty points and flexible payment terms. Offers worth paying margin for because they make each customer worth more: multi-pack tiers with a per-unit discount, subscribe and save, prepaid 90-day or annual plans at a deep discount (cash up front, longer commitment), and second-item or second-order discounts in the cart. Offers where brands 'die': a plain 10% off the hero product, which hands margin over for a small conversion bump and leaves the scaling problem unchanged; free shipping on a very low order value; and buy-one-get-one without unit economics that support it. The principle: a discount moves margin to the customer, while a good structure makes the customer worth more to you while giving them a better deal. How to apply: audit your current offers into these buckets, add the free ones, and replace flat hero discounts with structures that raise units, commitment or repeat.

claim: A pop-up offering 10% off that applies to one-time purchases undercuts a 20% subscription offer; make the pop-up offer the subscription offer itself.
body: A common leak in subscription brands is offer conflict between the email capture pop-up and the product page. The brand runs a strong subscription offer, say 20% off plus gifts, but the pop-up promises 10% off, and that code works on one-time purchase. Shoppers then compare 10% off with no commitment against 20% off with a commitment, and many take the one-time path, lowering first-order subscription take rate and the LTV that comes with it. The fix is congruence: the pop-up headline and the code should present the subscription offer (for example save 30% on your first subscription order plus a welcome kit), and the one-time purchase gets no discount and no incentive. The same principle extends to ads and email: every surface should name the same subscription-first offer. How to apply: list every discount the store shows (pop-up, banner, flows, ads), check which purchase type each code applies to, and remove or restrict any code that makes one-time purchase look like the better deal. The speaker calls this very underrated, but gave no measured lift, so watch take rate and first-order conversion rate separately after the change.
conditions: Subscription-led brands with an email or SMS capture pop-up and a discount code.
fails_when: Brands whose economics rely on one-time first orders (high-AOV, low-repeat products) or where the pop-up exists mainly to build a list for one-time buyers; removing the one-time incentive can lower overall first-order conversion.

claim: Customers whose first order is a subscription showed about 50% higher 6-month LTV ($195 vs $130), 2x at 12 months and 3x at 24 months, in one supplement brand's data.
body: The agency showed a single subscription brand's cohort report filtered by whether the first order carried a subscription. Month-6 LTV was about $130 for first orders without a subscription and about $195 for first orders with one, a 50% gap, widening to roughly 2x by month 12 and 3x by month 24. The speaker calls these bare-minimum numbers for a daily-use product. The mechanism is commitment and default behaviour: someone who starts on a subscription keeps receiving product unless they act, while a one-time buyer must decide to come back each time. The practical consequence is that first-order subscription take rate is the metric to optimise on the acquisition side, ahead of small CAC improvements. How to apply: in your subscription app or Klaviyo, split cohorts by first-order type and compare 6, 12 and 24 month revenue per customer; if the gap is large, prioritise take-rate levers on the product page and pop-up. Treat the gap as partly selection bias, since committed buyers self-select into subscription; the multiplier is not fully causal. Product fit matters: a daily powder retains far better than an occasional-use product such as seasonings or CBD gummies, so compare only against brands in the same consumption game.

claim: First-order subscription gifts should help the customer consume the product (frother, scoop, shaker); gifts of more of the same product drive skips and cancels.
body: The speaker says the main reason subscribers cancel is under-use: they either do not use the product enough to see results or they pile up too much of it. So welcome-kit gifts should make daily use easier, not add generic swag. Everyday Dose bundles a frother, a quality spoon and a creamer with the first subscription order; others include a shaker bottle. These items have low production cost, add stacked perceived value on the product page, and remove friction from the daily habit. A digital course or wellness booklet adds value at no unit cost. Later in the subscription, gifts can shift towards revenue expansion: sample packs of other SKUs that may become cross-sells, or branded items such as a tumbler. The one gift to avoid is extra units of the core product, because a customer with surplus stock delays or cancels the next order. Free samples of other products as the main welcome gift (AG1 style) can work but are weaker than consumption aids. How to apply: for each subscription SKU, list what makes using it daily awkward and pick a gift that solves it; reserve cross-sell samples for milestone orders.

claim: Match subscription cadence and quantity to real consumption; too much product is the most common cancel reason, so a 30-day cadence on a non-daily product guarantees churn.
body: Subscribers who accumulate unused product cancel, and they often say so in cancel surveys (too much product is described as usually the biggest reason). The cause is frequently the default plan rather than the customer: a 30-day subscription on something used a few times a week, or a fixed pack size that one person cannot finish. The speaker cites a beverage brand that keeps a 30-day cadence but lets the subscriber choose the number of cans, so a single person is not sent 48 cans a month. Daily products with 30 servings fit a 30-day cadence; anything else needs a different interval or a quantity selector. How to apply: compute servings per unit divided by realistic daily use to get the natural reorder interval, set the default frequency to that, and make quantity and frequency easy to adjust at signup and in the portal. Then read the cancel-reason data monthly; a rising share of too much product points to a cadence or onboarding problem (customers are not using it daily) rather than a price problem. Pair with onboarding that teaches the daily habit so the planned consumption rate actually happens.
conditions: Any subscription consumable; most acute for products not used every day.
fails_when: Products with a fixed, obvious daily dose where cadence already matches servings; there the remaining overstock usually comes from forgetting doses, which is an onboarding problem.

claim: A subscription base caps where monthly churn equals new subscribers: at 10% churn and 2,000 new a month, growth stops at 20,000 subscribers, so acquisition offers set the ceiling.
body: Matt Holman frames subscription growth as a stock and flow problem. Subscribers lost each month equal the active base times monthly churn; subscribers added equal new subscription orders. With 10% monthly churn and 2,000 new subscribers a month, a 10,000 base grows by 1,000 a month, but at 20,000 the 2,000 lost equal the 2,000 gained and the programme flatlines. The ceiling is new subscribers divided by churn rate, so you can raise it either way, but the effort differs. Lifting month-3 cohort retention from 60% to 65% or 70% takes months of gifts and messaging and touches only the customers still active; lifting subscriber opt-in rate on new orders from 40% to 45% through offer tests shows up within weeks and compounds on every future cohort. Offer tests also reveal which customers retain best, which itself lowers churn. How to apply: compute your ceiling as monthly new subscribers divided by monthly churn; if your active base is approaching it, put the next quarter's testing effort into offers and acquisition funnels, and track opt-in rate alongside churn. Note the speaker admits the line started as provocation; retention work still matters, it is just capped.
conditions: Subscription-led consumable brands with stable monthly churn; most relevant once the active base is approaching new adds divided by churn.
fails_when: Early brands with tiny bases far below the ceiling, or brands with very high churn caused by a product problem, where fixing retention or the product is the bigger lever.

If yes, a deep sitewide discount is not compatible, because suppression lists do not stop subscribers seeing ads and social posts. Then design the subscriber offer first and trickle down: for example 40% sitewide, but anything a subscriber adds to their next order during the sale is 50% off, or prepaying a three-month bundle earns two extra months. Push it through email with one-click add-to-next-order links (or interactive email tools such as Zamo) and the portal for new product drops, and tell the email and ad teams that the public offer should mention what subscribers get, which turns the sale into an acquisition offer for subscription. claim: Instead of deepening a subscription discount, give a catalog product whose landed cost is below the extra discount; 10% off a $100 item costs $10 per order.
body: Holman's rule for stacking value cheaply: compare the cash cost of a bigger discount with the landed cost of something you already sell. On a $100 product with 70% gross margin there is room to give value, but each extra 10% of discount costs $10 per order and teaches buyers to wait for discounts. Most brands with more than one SKU have an item, such as a sample pack, accessory or smaller product, with a landed cost under $5 or $10 that carries a higher perceived retail value. Giving that item with the subscription costs less than the discount, keeps the headline price intact, attracts buyers who want value rather than the lowest price, and introduces a second product that may become a cross-sell. Example offer: subscribe to protein powder and receive a 15-day electrolyte sample kit. How to apply: list every SKU and its landed cost; find items under the cash value of the discount step you were considering; test a gift-with-subscription arm against the deeper-discount arm and compare conversion rate, first-order margin and 90-day retention separately.

claim: On low-priced subscriptions, replace flat subscribe-and-save with buy-more-save-more tiers (one bag $45, two $80, three $120 on a $50 product) to lift value and deter discount hunters.
body: On a $20 product, 10% off is $2, which barely motivates anyone to commit to a subscription, and a pure discount message attracts buyers who are there only because it is cheaper. Holman's first test for single-SKU brands is a bulk or buy-more-save-more ladder layered on the subscription. His protein example on a $50 bag: one bag on subscription at $45 (10% off), two bags at $80 (an extra 10%, so $20 off instead of $10), three bags at $120. Three effects: more value is offered up front, so the offer reads as value not cheapness; buyers who only want the lowest price rarely commit to two or three bags, which filters out the most churn-prone customers; and the middle tier benefits from anchoring, feeling just right next to the three-bag option. Next tests for brands with more SKUs: a free sample kit of a second product for every subscriber, or a bundle builder of frequently bought-together items. Elevate (UK collagen) is cited for a gamified ladder where longer commitments unlock more items. How to apply: build two or three tiers, check contribution margin at each, and read conversion rate and LTV separately for each tier.
conditions: Single or few-SKU consumable subscriptions, especially under about $50 per unit.
fails_when: Products with short shelf life or bulky storage where multi-unit orders create overstock and later cancels; buyers on tight budgets may not convert at all on larger packs.

claim: Layer a pre-built starter kit on top of quantity breaks and make free gifts scale with units bought (one gift per bag), showing per-serving price on every tier.

Structure observed: 1) Subscription only, no one-time option. 2) Choose variant (flavour) first. 3) Choose starter kit (product plus low-cost, high-perceived-value accessories such as mugs) or product alone. 4) Quantity break of 1, 2 or 3 bags with savings rising per tier (shown as 62, 100 and 153 off). 5) Gifts unlock with quantity: one mug per bag, or at Jaby one gift at one or two bottles, three gifts at three, four at four. 6) Every tier shows a per-serving or per-unit price (for example 24 per bag, 15.95 per bottle) to remove sticker shock on the larger bundle. 7) Support with free shipping, skip or cancel any time, a delivery date, a 60-day money-back guarantee and an on-page upgrade to a day-and-night kit. The check: take AOV in store currency, multiply by conversion rate with the percent sign dropped. An 80 AOV at 3.2% gives 256, which passes; a 45 AOV at 2.5% gives 112.5, which means offer, pricing and page work comes before more spend. Mathematically the score divided by 100 is revenue per session, so 250 means roughly 2.50 per landing-page session. How to apply: 1) Pull AOV and session conversion rate for paid cold traffic only, not blended with returning buyers. 2) Compute the score per landing page or product page. 3) Below 250, raise AOV first with quantity breaks, starter bundles, on-page upsells and cart cross-sells, then work conversion rate. 4) Above 250, keep pushing it, because each step up lifts the spend ceiling. The benchmark is stated as a rule from the agency's client work (clients cited at about 9 million revenue in 12 months) with no sample or cost-per-click context, and the source switches between pounds and dollars, so treat 250 as a rough screen, not a target computed from your own CPCs.

claim: Space bundle savings so the middle pack saves as much over the single as the large pack saves over the middle; one test reported +11.7% conversion and about +5% AOV.
body: The agency restructured a one, three and five pack ladder for Wildman Drinking. Before, the three pack saved $10 and the five pack $20 versus singles, so each step up looked like a similar small gain. Knowing that few buyers needed five units but many bought three (for themselves and a couple of friends), they re-spaced the savings so stepping from one to three saved $20, and stepping from three to five saved a further $20. The three pack now captured the same incremental saving as the much larger commitment, making it look like the obvious sweet spot, while the five pack acted as the anchor. Reported results: 11.74% higher conversion rate and roughly 5% higher AOV and revenue per visitor. In the same test they also raised the compare-at reference prices while keeping selling prices unchanged, which they credit for a higher perceived deal. claim: Longer guarantees (one year to lifetime) are argued to cause fewer returns than 30 to 90 day ones, which keep buyers watching the return deadline.
body: Whitman's argument: every purchase carries stress between paying and experiencing the product, and the bigger the price the bigger the stress. A guarantee shifts the balance from skepticism toward the wish to believe. He claims, citing unnamed studies, that short windows (30, 60 or 90 days) keep customers in a 'beat the clock' mindset where they judge the product against the deadline and send it back in time, while long ones (six months, a year, five or ten years, lifetime) signal confidence and remove the deadline pressure, so returns can actually fall. The classic proof point is Hormel's Depression-era 'double your money back' soup offer: executives feared mass abuse, yet only 12 women claimed it and the ad sold well. How to apply: offer the longest, strongest guarantee your margins and return data can support, ideally longer than every competitor; display it prominently (a certificate-style border and a signature on ads, product pages and inserts); and use the gap in copy ('why do competitors guarantee theirs for only 90 days?'). claim: Free samples or trials pay only when the prospect requests them and makes some effort (form, email, small fee); unrequested samples lose value, per Claude Hopkins.
body: Hopkins, the copywriter behind Scientific Advertising, wrote that he never found it profitable to hand samples to people who had not asked for them; goods given away without asking lose respect, while a small effort from the buyer creates interest before the product arrives. The podcast host maps this to modern funnels: the effort can be filling in a form, giving an email, or claiming a trial through an ad. It pairs with Hopkins' other repeated point that a good product demonstrated is its own best salesman, and with the Estee Lauder story of moving advertising money into free samples. How to apply in ecommerce: 1) Do not mass-mail samples or insert unrequested items to cold lists. 2) Gate the sample behind a request: a sample-pack landing page, email or SMS capture, a quiz, or a small shipping charge. 3) Credit any sample fee against the first full-size order so the effort feels returned. 4) Follow up every sample request with a purchase path (email flow, discount for full size within a set number of days). 5) Track sample-to-paid conversion by acquisition source to see whether the effort barrier filters for real buyers. claim: Give samples free and only to people who ask after reading your claims; charging even a token fee or offering half-price trials cut replies sharply in Hopkins' keyed tests.
body: Hopkins tracked mail-order and coupon ads down to the cost per reply and cost per customer, and his sampling rules come from those keyed returns. First, a sample requested after reading the ad is worth far more than one handed out cold: the requester already knows the claims and looks for the qualities promised, while an unasked-for sample gets little attention. Second, the word 'free' itself multiplies readership, so samples often pay for themselves through cheaper replies before any sale. Third, charging a dime or a stamp for the sample raised the cost per reply by 40 cents to $1 in his accounts and, he estimates, three in four to nine in ten prospects refuse to pay. Fourth, part-price trial offers ('buy one, we buy the other', coupons for part of the price) did not pay in keyed tests; before a prospect is convinced, half price is about as hard to get as full price. Fifth, if a small sample is not a fair test of the product, pay for a full-size package rather than stop short. Modern use: compare a free sample (pay shipping or not) gated behind a claim-led page against paid trial kits, judging by cost per eventual customer, not cost per request.

claim: When usage data shows a subscriber is overstocked, email them proactively to pause or skip, giving up a shipment rather than waiting for a fatigue cancellation.
body: Subscription churn often starts with a pile-up: the customer receives product faster than they use it, feels they are wasting money, and cancels outright. The standard response, making cancellation hard, buys a month or two and costs trust. The wild bet is the reverse: watch the signals that a subscriber is overstocked and tell them to pause before they ask. Signals include skipped or delayed consumption indicators, repeated 'skip' clicks, support messages about having too much, or a delivery cadence shorter than the product's realistic use time for that household. Steps: (1) in the subscription app (Recharge or similar), set a rule for subscribers whose cadence exceeds expected use, or who skipped twice; (2) send a plain, personal email suggesting a one-cycle pause or longer interval, with a one-click link; (3) make pause, skip and cadence change as easy as cancellation; (4) compare 6- and 12-month retention for those who received the email against a holdout. The source cites a fitness platform and a candle brand that gained retention from flexibility, without comparable data, so measure your own.

claim: A 30% discount can triple break-even ROAS: a $100 order at 40% gross margin breaks even at 2.5x, but at $70 with unchanged $60 costs needs about 7x.
body: Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by gross margin percentage, and break-even CAC equals gross profit in dollars on the order. Discounts cut price but not cost, so they shrink gross margin far faster than the headline percentage. The speaker's example: a $100 product with $60 of cost of delivery has $40 gross margin, so break-even ROAS is 2.5 and break-even CAC is $40. At 30% off, the price is $70, costs stay $60, gross margin falls to $10 (about 14%; he rounds the ratio to 10%), break-even ROAS rises to roughly 7 to 10, and break-even CAC drops to $10, which almost no paid channel can hit, so that discount should not be used for new-customer acquisition. Run this math before any promotion: if a 20% discount means efficiency must jump from 2x to 12x, the extra demand will not cover it. Cheaper ways to offer value: bundles, because a second unit raises shipping and fulfilment cost by roughly 20% rather than doubling it, so margin can be shared without lowering margin percentage; and gift with purchase, such as a bag with a $4 cost shown as worth $50 on a two-towel order, which doubles AOV for little margin. Deep straight discounts belong on slow grade C stock you need to turn back into cash.

claim: Recompute break-even ROAS for every discount depth before the sale; required ROAS rises steeply because discounts eat gross margin, not revenue (speaker: 2.0 becomes 4.5 at 40% off).
body: Break-even ROAS equals 1 divided by gross margin, where gross margin is profit after cost of goods, fulfilment and payment fees as a share of the discounted price. A discount reduces price while costs stay the same, so margin falls proportionally much faster than price, and the required ROAS rises steeply, not linearly, with discount depth. Blue Sense Digital's example: a brand breaking even at 2.0 ROAS needs about 4.5 at a 40% discount. The exact figure depends on cost structure; with a pure 50% product margin and no other costs, a 40% discount leaves about 17% margin and a break-even near 6, so always compute it from your own numbers. How to apply: list each planned offer (site-wide %, tiered, gift with purchase, free shipping), compute gross margin per order under each, convert to break-even and target ROAS, and load those targets into the pacing sheet. The agency will not set Black Friday efficiency targets without the discount and gross margin figures. Also decide whether the sale is a profit play or a stock-clearance play, since clearance can justify spending past break-even.

fails_when: Gift-with-purchase offers using dead stock, where the cost is not a cash margin cut in the same way; inventory clearance goals that accept negative contribution.

claim: Scarcity persuades most when it is new (stock dropped from plenty to few) and caused by other buyers' demand; constant or accidental scarcity works far less.
body: In Worchel's cookie experiment, a cookie from a jar of two was rated more desirable than the same cookie from a jar of ten, which is the familiar scarcity effect. Two further findings set the conditions. First, people whose jar went from ten cookies to two rated the cookies higher than people who had two all along: a drop from plenty to few beats permanent shortage. Second, among the newly scarce group, those told the cookies had been taken to meet other participants' demand rated them highest of all, higher than those told the reduction was a mistake. Competition for a limited item adds to its pull. Store application: (1) show stock or capacity signals only when they are real and changing, such as 'restocked last week, 70 percent sold', a live count that falls, or a waitlist size; (2) explain why stock is short when it is because other buyers bought it ('sold out twice this month'); (3) retire permanent 'only 3 left' banners and evergreen countdown timers, which are constant scarcity at best and fake at worst; (4) use restock and back-in-stock emails, which naturally carry the abundance-to-scarcity shift.

claim: Show a larger, realistic offer first and retreat to the smaller one: rejection-then-retreat lifted agreement from 17% to 50%, but backfires if the first ask looks unreasonable.
body: When a request is refused and the asker then makes a smaller one, people treat the second as a concession and feel obliged to reciprocate; the smaller request also looks smaller by contrast. In Cialdini's field experiment, 17 percent of students agreed to chaperone young offenders on a zoo trip when asked directly; when they were first asked to counsel an offender two hours a week for two years and refused, then offered the zoo trip, 50 percent agreed. A further study cited in the book found the tactic fails when the first request is so extreme it seems illegitimate, because the retreat is not seen as a real concession. Store application: (1) on post-purchase upsell pages, lead with the larger bundle or subscription, and if declined, follow immediately with a smaller add-on framed as the alternative; (2) on product pages, present the premium tier or bigger bundle first so the core option reads as the reasonable choice; (3) keep the first offer plausible for that buyer, roughly within a few times the cart value, not an absurd anchor. Track take rate on the second offer and refund rate, since buyers who feel pushed return more.
conditions: Post-purchase one-click upsell flows, quantity and bundle tiers, sales and support conversations; offers where a bigger and a smaller version both make sense.
fails_when: The first offer is clearly irrelevant or wildly overpriced for the buyer (seen as manipulation, no reciprocity), buyers already know the price ladder well, or repeated decline-then-offer screens make checkout feel like a trap and raise refunds.
numbers: 17 percent direct agreement vs 50 percent after a refused larger request (about 3x)

claim: A 'was' price is genuine only if the item was openly offered at it, in good faith, for a reasonable recent time; a price inflated to create a markdown, never offered, or cut right after being set is fictitious.
body: The FTC's Guides Against Deceptive Pricing (16 CFR 233.1) say a former price comparison is fine when the former price is the actual, bona fide price at which the item was offered to the public on a regular basis for a reasonably substantial period. A price can be genuine even with few sales at it, if it was openly offered in good faith in the ordinary course of business, but the ad should not imply it was a selling price unless substantial sales happened. It is fictitious when it was set artificially high to allow a large advertised cut, when the item was never offered at that price, when it was used only in the distant past without saying so, or when it was cut right after being set. The rule's example: pens normally at 7.50 briefly listed at 10 with few sales, then advertised as 'Were 10, now 7.50', is a false bargain. How to apply: before writing 'was' or 'save X', check the price history on the store and use only a price really charged recently.
conditions: US ads and product pages that compare to a former price.
fails_when: State laws and other countries' rules differ in the time period required; check local rules for each market.

claim: US law on online subscriptions requires clear disclosure of all material terms before taking billing details, express informed consent before charging, and a simple way to stop recurring charges.
body: The Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, 15 U.S.C. 8403, makes it unlawful to charge a consumer through an online negative option (auto-renewing) sale unless the seller clearly and conspicuously discloses all material terms before obtaining billing information, obtains express informed consent before charging, and provides simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges. For a subscribe-and-save offer this means the price after any first-order discount, the frequency, and how to cancel are shown before checkout, the buyer actively agrees to the subscription, and cancelling online is easy. Some US states add their own auto-renewal rules on top.
conditions: US buyers on auto-renewing subscriptions sold online.
fails_when: State auto-renewal laws can be stricter; this card does not cover them. Not legal advice.

claim: In India, a recurring card charge needs an e-mandate registered with extra authentication, a pre-debit notice at least 24 hours before each charge, and lets the buyer opt out or withdraw at any time.
body: The RBI circular of 21 August 2019 on e-mandates for recurring card transactions says a mandate is registered only after successful additional factor authentication, the issuer must notify the cardholder at least 24 hours before each debit, and the cardholder may opt out of that charge or the whole mandate, and withdraw any mandate online at any time. Charges above a per-transaction cap need authentication each time; the 2019 cap was 2,000 rupees and RBI has revised it since, so check the current circular. claim: In the US a brand may suggest a retail price and, acting alone, stop supplying dealers who ignore it; agreed minimum resale prices are judged under a rule of reason federally but are illegal per se in some states.
body: The FTC's guide on manufacturer-imposed requirements says reasonable price, territory and customer restrictions on dealers can be lawful because they can help competition between brands. A suggested retail price leaves the dealer free to set its own price, and a manufacturer acting on its own may adopt a take-it-or-leave-it policy and stop dealing with retailers that do not follow it; what is unlawful is a collective agreement among competitors. Since a 2007 Supreme Court decision, manufacturer-imposed minimum resale price programmes are evaluated under a rule of reason, but some state antitrust laws and international authorities treat minimum price rules as illegal per se. Territorial and customer restrictions imposed by the manufacturer alone are generally legal. How to use it: write wholesale terms with a suggested retail price or a unilateral advertised price policy, not a signed promise from the retailer to sell at or above a price, and have a lawyer check the states and countries involved.
conditions: US federal antitrust guidance as published by the FTC on the date fetched; state law and other countries differ.
fails_when: The policy is agreed with or among retailers, enforced through coordination with competitors, or used in a state or country that bans minimum resale prices outright.

claim: A US 'free with purchase' offer must rest on the paid item's regular price, not raised to cover the gift, with terms stated at the outset.
body: A US 'free with purchase' offer must rest on the paid item's regular price, not raised to cover the gift, with terms stated at the outset, and one product size should not carry a free offer more than 6 months in any 12. The FTC's guide on the word 'Free' (16 CFR 251.1) says a free item offered with a purchase is judged against the regular price of the item the buyer must pay for. The regular price is the price at which the item was openly and actively sold, in the same quantity and quality, in the trade area for at least 30 days; if few sales happened at that price, the free offer is not proper (introductory offers are an exception). The seller may not recover the gift's cost by raising that price, cutting quality or shrinking quantity. All conditions must be stated clearly and conspicuously at the outset; an asterisk to a footnote does not count. So that a free offer stays special, one size of a product should not carry a free offer in a trade area for more than 6 months in any 12-month period, at least 30 days should pass between such offers, no more than three may run there in 12 months, and sales of that size under the offer should not exceed half of its sales there. How to apply: before a gift-with-purchase, confirm the paid item's price has been stable for 30 days and stays the same during the offer, write the threshold and gift terms next to the offer, and log each free offer on the yearly calendar so no product runs one more than 6 months a year.
conditions: US stores advertising a free gift or free item conditional on a purchase.
fails_when: Outside the US the rules differ; state laws may add rules; the guide is FTC guidance on what is deceptive, so a lawyer should confirm edge cases.

claim: In the US, say 'money back guarantee' or 'satisfaction guarantee' only if the store refunds the full purchase price when the buyer asks, and state any material condition clearly in the ad itself.
body: The FTC's Guides for the Advertising of Warranties and Guarantees (16 CFR 239.3) say terms such as 'Satisfaction Guarantee', 'Money Back Guarantee' and 'Free Trial Offer' should be used only when the seller refunds the full purchase price of the advertised product at the purchaser's request. An ad that mentions such a guarantee should clearly and prominently disclose any material limitation or condition, for example that only the unused part must be returned within 30 days, or that the product must come back in its original package. How to apply: if the store keeps outbound shipping, charges a restocking fee, requires the item unopened, or gives store credit instead of money, either drop those conditions or stop calling it a money-back guarantee and state the exact terms next to the claim on the product page, cart and ads.
conditions: US ads, product pages and emails that mention a satisfaction or money-back guarantee.
fails_when: Other countries' consumer laws set their own minimum rights; Magnuson-Moss written warranty rules add duties for consumer products with written warranties; confirm complex cases with a lawyer.

claim: A US 'lifetime' guarantee must clearly say whose or what lifetime it covers, such as the original buyer's ownership or the product's life.
body: The FTC's guide on 'lifetime' and similar representations (16 CFR 239.4) advises that an ad using 'lifetime', 'life' or similar words for a warranty or guarantee should clearly and prominently disclose the life the promise refers to, for example the life of the product or the time the original purchaser owns it. claim: From 1 January 2027, any announced price cut on an Indian e-commerce site must show the prior price, meaning the lowest price offered in the 30 days before the announcement, and sponsored listings must be clearly labelled.
body: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026 were notified on 9 September 2026 and take effect on 1 January 2027, according to Poovayya & Co. Under new Rule 4(13), when an e-commerce entity announces a price reduction it must show the reduced price next to a prior price, which is the lowest price at which the item was offered in the 30 days before the announcement. Rule 4(12) requires sponsored listings to be clearly and prominently identified as such, and Rule 4(11)(c) bars manipulating search results or indexes in a misleading way. The authors note the rules do not deal with newly listed products, personalised pricing or layered discounts. How to apply: keep a daily price log per SKU; before any sale, set the strikethrough or compare-at price to the lowest price charged in the previous 30 days, not a list price or MRP you rarely charged; and label paid placements on your own site or app.
conditions: E-commerce entities and sellers announcing discounts to consumers in India from 1 January 2027.
fails_when: New products with under 30 days of history, personalised prices and stacked discounts are not addressed. This summary is from a law firm, so check the gazette text before relying on clause numbers.

claim: India's dark pattern guidelines cover false scarcity or popularity claims, advertising one product then pushing a pricier one, shaming decline buttons, ads made to look like user posts or news, and repeated unpermitted prompts.
body: Khaitan & Co.'s summary of the CCPA's 2023 dark patterns guidelines describes five patterns that sit in offers, ads and pop-ups. False urgency is creating a false sense of popularity or scarcity to pressure a purchase, such as saying the chosen item is the last one in stock. Bait and switch is advertising one product to draw a buyer in and then delivering a different, often pricier one, for example showing an item as available, then saying it is out of stock and offering a costlier substitute. Confirm shaming uses fear, shame or guilt to push a choice, such as a decline button that reads 'I will stay unsecured'. Disguised advertisement is masking ads as user-generated content or news articles; the seller or advertiser is responsible for the disclosure, and the 2022 misleading advertisement guidelines also apply. Nagging is repeatedly interrupting users with requests for commercial gain, such as prompts to enable notifications or accept cookies, unless the user has allowed them. How to apply: tie every stock or 'X people viewing' counter to live data; only run a countdown when the offer really ends at zero and does not reset; keep advertised items in stock or pause the ad; write neutral decline text; label creator and advertorial content as ads; and cap repeat pop-ups once a user says no.
conditions: Ads, landing pages, apps and websites selling to consumers in India.
fails_when: The summary gives no rule on countdown timers by name; the timer advice applies the false urgency definition. ASCI's ad rules on the same patterns also apply. This is a law-firm summary.

claim: India's dark pattern guidelines treat four things as drip pricing: price not shown upfront, a higher charge after confirmation, 'free' without saying continued use needs payment, and blocking a paid service until more is bought.
body: Annexure 1 of the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (30 November 2023) defines drip pricing in four forms: elements of the price not revealed upfront or revealed surreptitiously; a price after purchase confirmation higher than the amount shown at checkout; a product or service advertised as free without saying that continued use needs an in-app purchase; and stopping a user from using a service already paid for unless something more is bought. The illustrations include a flight shown at one price at checkout and charged at another at payment, a 'play chess for free' app that asks for payment after 7 days without saying so, and a gym membership that turns out to need special shoes or gloves. A marketplace is not liable for price changes made by third-party sellers or caused by factors beyond its control. How to apply: show delivery, COD and platform fees on the product page or before the cart total, keep the payment amount identical to the checkout total, and state any time limit on free trials or samples in the offer itself.
conditions: Platforms, advertisers and sellers offering goods or services to buyers in India.
fails_when: Price changes by a third-party seller on a marketplace (marketplace exception); the illustrations are guidance, not an exhaustive legal test.

claim: India's 2023 dark pattern guidelines ban false urgency: invented scarcity or popularity, such as fake 'people viewing' counts, or a 'limited time, select group' sale that is not limited.
body: The CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 define false urgency as falsely stating or implying urgency or scarcity to push a user into an immediate purchase or action, including showing false popularity of a product or overstating how few units remain. The illustrations are showing high demand without basis (for example, a rooms-left alert with an invented count of people viewing) and creating false time pressure, such as calling a sale exclusive for a limited time to a select group of users when it is not. The guidelines apply to every platform offering goods or services in India, and to advertisers and sellers. Countdown timers, low-stock badges and 'X people bought this' widgets are fine only when they show real data: the timer ends the offer when it reaches zero, the stock count is live, and the viewer or sales count is genuine. How to apply: audit every urgency widget on the store (many apps fake them by default), switch off any that do not read live data, and end sales when the timer says they end.
conditions: Product pages, carts, emails and ads seen by buyers in India.
fails_when: Genuine limited stock or time-bound offers that are honestly stated; ASCI's 2023 ad guidelines also require stock evidence for scarcity claims in ads.

claim: In India, adding paid items, services or donations at checkout without consent is basket sneaking; free samples, complimentary services and disclosed necessary fees (delivery, gift wrap, taxes) are allowed.
body: Annexure 1 of the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 defines basket sneaking as including extra items such as products, services or payments to charity or donation at checkout without the user's consent, so the total goes above what was chosen. Free samples, complimentary services and necessary fees disclosed at the time of purchase do not count; the guidelines name delivery charges, gift wrapping charges and government taxes as examples of such fees. Illustrations include pre-ticked paid add-ons, a paid subscription added to a single-service booking, and travel insurance added to a flight. A related pattern, confirm shaming, covers using guilt or ridicule to push the add-on, such as a decline button that says 'I will stay unsecured' or mocking a shopper who removes a charity donation. How to apply: present upsells, protection plans and donations as unticked options the shopper adds, word the decline neutrally ('No thanks'), and put any free gift in the cart at zero price with a note that it is free.
conditions: Checkout, cart and order-bump flows for buyers in India.
fails_when: Fees that are necessary and disclosed at purchase; add-ons the shopper actively chooses.

claim: India's dark pattern guidelines ban subscription traps (hard or hidden cancellation, card details for a free trial) and covert SaaS billing (no notice when a trial turns paid, silent renewals).
body: Annexure 1 of the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 defines a subscription trap as making cancellation of a paid subscription impossible or long and complex, hiding the cancel option, forcing a user to give payment details or authorise auto-debit to get a free subscription, or giving ambiguous or cumbersome cancellation instructions. SaaS billing covers recurring charges that exploit subscription loops to take money as quietly as possible: not telling the user when a free trial converts to paid, silent recurring debits or auto-renewals, charging for features the user does not use, and shady card authorisation. Both apply to subscribe-and-save, refill clubs and memberships, not only software. RBI's e-mandate rules (see the library's recurring payments card) separately require a pre-debit notice. How to apply: put a cancel link where the shopper manages the subscription, let them cancel in as few steps as they took to sign up, email before a trial converts and before each renewal, and take card details for a trial only if the offer says clearly that it will convert.
conditions: Subscriptions, memberships, trials and auto-renewing plans sold to buyers in India.
fails_when: One-off purchases; illustrations are guidance and the CCPA decides close cases.

claim: Under India's 2022 ad guidelines, a low-price bait ad needs enough stock or a 'limited stock' note, and 'free' is barred if the buyer pays packing or handling, or the base price rose to fund it.
body: Clause 5 of the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements, 2022 covers bait advertisements, which lure buyers with a low price. The advertiser must have a realistic prospect of selling at that price, keep enough supply for foreseeable demand, say stock is limited if demand may exceed it, say so if it is testing demand, and disclose any geographic or age restrictions. Clause 7 covers free claims: an item cannot be called free or without charge if the buyer pays more than the unavoidable cost of responding and receiving it, the commitment needed to get it must be clear, and 'free' is not allowed where the buyer pays packing or handling, where the price of the required purchase went up because of the promotion, or where its quality or quantity went down. An element already included in a package price cannot be called free, and 'free trial' cannot describe a money-back offer or one that needs a non-refundable purchase. How to apply: cost every 'free gift' and 'buy 2 get 1' offer at the normal price of the paid item, never add handling fees to a free item, and add 'while stocks last' with real stock behind it.
conditions: Promotions and price ads seen by buyers in India.
fails_when: ASCI's code adds its own free and BOGO rules (see the ASCI card); delivery charges at the actual cost of sending are allowed if disclosed.
